title: 6.1.1 Plan: Break Pocket into parts
description: Before any code: list the parts of Pocket, what the game must remember between frames, what to build first and what looks hard. AI-graded with hints.
unit: 6.1 Pocket: plan and the aim line

aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is on this page: go back and reread it if you get stuck. A few short sentences per answer is plenty, in your own everyday words.

You are about to build Pocket. Before you write any code, plan it.

1. List at least four separate parts of the game, things it has or does.

2. Which two or more things does the game have to remember from one frame to the next?

3. Which part would you build first, so something runs today, and why?

4. Which part are you unsure how to build, and what makes it hard?

rubric.title: Four or more parts of the game are named
rubric.description: The student names about four parts of Pocket in their own words, such as the table, the cue ball, the aim line, pulling back and letting go, the pockets, counting shots. Credit any list, however loose, short or oddly worded; a list of fewer than four still gets full credit if it clearly tries. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Do not mark this criterion missing just because the student skipped this numbered question: when the response is about Pocket at all, even if it only describes the game or says how they feel about it, mark this criterion met. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.

rubric.title: Says what the game must remember between frames
rubric.description: The student names at least two things the game has to remember from one frame to the next, for example where the ball is, how fast it is going, whether the pointer is held down, or how many shots have been taken. Any sensible item, or any gesture at remembering something, earns full credit. Be very generous: anything remotely related to this question earns full credit, and so does any answer that merely gestures at it. Read the student's whole response, not only the line that answers this question: if anything anywhere in it touches this question, even indirectly, give full credit. Only a blank response, or one about something else entirely, is a miss.
